case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, under AEDPA, the Maryland appellate court unreasonably applied clearly established Supreme Court Brady materiality precedent by treating materiality like a sufficiency-of-the-evidence inquiry rather than assessing the suppressed evidence’s cumulative effect on the entire case.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1) (AEDPA standard for federal habeas relief) as applied to the Due Process Clause Brady doctrine (Brady v. Maryland) governing disclosure of exculpatory and impeachment evidence.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (state officials) argue that the state appellate court properly denied Brady relief because the withheld evidence was not material in light of the remaining trial evidence supporting the verdict, and that—even if federal courts might weigh things differently—AEDPA requires deference because fairminded jurists could agree with the state court’s assessment; they rely in part on readings of Kyles/Strickler suggesting strong remaining evidence defeats materiality.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Martin) argues that clearly established Supreme Court law (especially Kyles) requires a holistic, cumulative materiality analysis that adds the suppressed evidence to the defense case and subtracts its impeachment force from the prosecution case, and that the Maryland appellate court unreasonably applied that rule by effectively using a sufficiency-style 'other evidence was enough' rationale; Martin further contends Strickler is factually distinguishable because impeachment of the key witness here would have significantly weakened the prosecution’s remaining evidence and theory (including how the prosecution argued the case and how instructions were framed).

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s Richter/Andrade point is the strongest for the petitioner: AEDPA deference targets the state court’s result, and we cannot convert Kyles into a federal opinion-writing mandate or redo materiality de novo. But Justice Barrett persuasively identifies the limiting principle under Williams v. Taylor: habeas relief may be warranted where the state court, in substance, employs a materially different analytic framework—here, treating the “remaining evidence is strong” inventory as effectively dispositive rather than integrating the suppressed evidence’s cumulative impeachment/exculpatory force into the case as tried, which Kyles forbids as a sufficiency proxy. Richter tolerates thin reasoning, not use of the wrong yardstick; on this record, the methodological departure is not merely debatable weighing but an unreasonable application of clearly established law. A narrow holding can emphasize that considering residual strength is permissible, but not as a substitute for Kyles’s cumulative, whole-case materiality assessment.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: I remain unpersuaded that § 2254(d)(1) is satisfied. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett argue that Maryland used the “wrong yardstick” under Williams v. Taylor by treating “remaining evidence” as dispositive, but Kyles does not clearly establish a categorical prohibition on weighing the untainted record as part of assessing whether suppressed evidence undermines confidence in the verdict; materiality necessarily looks to the whole trial record. Richter and Lockyer, as Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, direct us to review the reasonableness of the state court’s adjudication, not to parse its analytic sequence or demand an explicit “cumulative narrative” discussion, so long as the court substantively addressed the Bagley/Strickler “reasonable probability” question. Given that fairminded jurists could view the withheld impeachment as insufficient to create a reasonable probability of a different result, I would reverse rather than convert Kyles into an opinion-writing or methodology-enforcement rule on habeas.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take seriously Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s reliance on Williams v. Taylor for the proposition that a state court can unreasonably apply clearly established law by using the wrong framework, and I agree Kyles rejects treating Brady as a sufficiency-of-the-evidence test. But Richter and Lockyer require us to ask whether the state court’s adjudication is beyond fairminded disagreement, not whether its opinion integrated the suppressed evidence in the narrative, cumulative fashion we would prefer; Kyles does not clearly establish that discussion of the “remaining evidence” is categorically improper in the Bagley/Strickler “reasonable probability” inquiry. Justice Sotomayor’s methodological-error critique, in my view, risks converting Kyles into an AEDPA-enforceable opinion-writing mandate and inviting federal reweighing, when reasonable jurists could still conclude—even accounting for added impeachment—that confidence in the verdict was not undermined. Because that conclusion remains at least fairly debatable on this record, § 2254(d)(1) bars relief.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s Richter/Andrade point—that AEDPA deference attaches to the result and we cannot police opinion-writing—does not resolve the antecedent Williams v. Taylor question whether Maryland used the correct Brady yardstick in substance. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett explain, Kyles rejects a materiality analysis that functionally becomes a sufficiency-style inventory of “remaining evidence” without integrating the suppressed evidence’s cumulative impeachment/exculpatory force into the whole-case picture; Richter tolerates terse reasoning, not a methodological collapse into the very approach Kyles forbids. Justice Thomas is right that Kyles permits considering the whole record, including residual strength, but here the court’s analysis treated residual strength as dispositive rather than asking whether the suppressed evidence would reasonably undermine confidence in the verdict as tried. Given the real-world stakes for a defendant denied evidence central to testing the State’s case, I cannot say this was within fairminded disagreement under § 2254(d)(1).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh press the best objection: under Richter/Andrade, §2254(d)(1) deference attaches to results and we cannot turn Kyles into an opinion-writing mandate or reweigh the record. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett correctly identify the narrower, Williams v. Taylor path: a state court can unreasonably apply clearly established law by using a materially different analytic framework in substance, even while reciting “undermine confidence.” Here, the Maryland court’s treatment functionally makes residual strength dispositive without integrating the suppressed evidence’s cumulative impeachment/exculpatory force into the case as tried—the sufficiency-like shortcut Kyles rejects—so Richter’s tolerance for thin reasoning does not insulate a wrong yardstick. That keeps the inquiry tethered to governing law rather than to preferred judicial prose, and it places the decision beyond fairminded disagreement under §2254(d)(1).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is that Richter/Andrade demand deference to the state court’s result and forbid habeas courts from policing opinion-writing or reweighing close evidence. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett persuasively emphasize, Williams v. Taylor makes clear that § 2254(d)(1) is satisfied when the state court, in substance, employs a materially different legal framework—even if it recites the right verbal formula. Kyles clearly establishes that Brady materiality is a cumulative, whole-case inquiry and “not a sufficiency of the evidence test”; when the state court’s analysis functionally treats residual strength as dispositive without integrating the suppressed evidence’s combined impeachment/exculpatory force, that is a yardstick error Richter does not insulate. Under a textual, result-focused AEDPA approach, the key is not the opinion’s elegance but whether the adjudication applied the right governing rule; here it did not, beyond fairminded disagreement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s “wrong yardstick” argument is the strongest counter: under Williams, a state court can unreasonably apply clearly established law even while reciting the right standard, and Kyles rejects a sufficiency-of-the-evidence proxy. But Richter/Andrade still require us to ask whether the state court’s adjudication was beyond fairminded disagreement, and Kyles does not clearly establish that emphasizing the strength of the remaining evidence—while imperfectly integrating the suppressed material—is categorically a forbidden framework rather than a permissible part of the Bagley/Strickler “undermine confidence” inquiry. I do not read the Maryland decision as making residual strength dispositive in a way no fairminded jurist could endorse; at most it reflects arguable misemphasis, and elevating that into a § 2254(d)(1) violation risks converting Kyles into a habeas-enforceable opinion-writing or analytic-format requirement. For institutional and AEDPA reasons, I would reverse because this is still within the realm of reasonable disagreement about cumulative materiality on the full record.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—echoed by Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Thomas—is that Richter/Andrade require deference to results and forbid converting Kyles into a habeas-enforced opinion-writing mandate. But, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Williams v. Taylor permits § 2254(d)(1) relief when the state court substantively applies a materially different framework, and Kyles clearly establishes that Brady materiality is not satisfied by an inventory of inculpatory “remaining evidence” untethered from the cumulative effect of the suppression on the case as tried. Richter tolerates thin or even opaque reasoning; it does not insulate a decision that, in operation, uses the sufficiency-style yardstick Kyles rejected. Because Maryland’s analysis functionally treated residual strength as dispositive rather than integrating the withheld impeachment/exculpation cumulatively, the adjudication falls beyond fairminded disagreement under clearly established law.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point—grounded in Richter/Andrade—that AEDPA deference attaches to results and tolerates imperfect state-court reasoning does not resolve the distinct Williams v. Taylor problem here: a state court can unreasonably apply clearly established law by using a materially different analytic yardstick. I agree with the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett that the Maryland court’s analysis functionally mirrors the sufficiency-style “remaining evidence was strong” inventory Kyles rejected, because it did not integrate the suppressed evidence’s cumulative impeachment/exculpatory force into the case as tried and instead treated residual strength as dispositive. Richter protects reasonable applications of the correct framework; it does not insulate a decision that collapses Brady materiality into “still enough evidence,” which is a methodological error with concrete fairness consequences for a criminal defendant. On that narrow ground, § 2254(d)(1) is satisfied without imposing an opinion-writing requirement or relitigating materiality de novo.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), we owe substantial deference to the state court, and relief is barred unless its decision was beyond the bounds of fairminded disagreement. But Kyles v. Whitley clearly establishes that Brady materiality is not a sufficiency-of-the-evidence test and must be assessed cumulatively, by considering how the suppressed evidence would have affected the whole evidentiary picture rather than asking whether the remaining evidence could still support the verdict. If the Maryland appellate court effectively treated “other evidence is strong” as dispositive and failed to evaluate the withheld evidence’s combined impeachment/exculpatory force against the prosecution’s case as tried, that is an unreasonable application of Kyles even under Harrington v. Richter’s demanding standard. A narrow affirmance for respondent is appropriate on the limited ground that the state court’s mode of analysis contravened the clearly established cumulative-materiality framework.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), federal habeas relief is barred unless the state court’s decision was not merely wrong but an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established law, and AEDPA demands substantial deference to state-court adjudications. Although Kyles v. Whitley states Brady materiality “is not a sufficiency of evidence test,” the question here is whether the Maryland court’s reasoning crossed the AEDPA line; even if its discussion emphasized the strength of remaining evidence, fairminded jurists could still conclude the suppressed report did not create a “reasonable probability” of a different result under Bagley/Strickler when the record is considered as a whole. Harrington v. Richter and Lockyer v. Andrade instruct that § 2254(d)(1) protects state decisions within the bounds of reasonable disagreement, and I cannot say the state court’s application was so erroneous as to be beyond those bounds. Respecting the Constitution’s allocation of criminal justice primarily to the States, I would reverse the grant of habeas relief.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a federal court may grant relief only if the state court’s decision was an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law, not merely incorrect. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Harrington v. Richter. Although Kyles v. Whitley emphasizes that Brady materiality “is not a sufficiency of evidence test” and requires considering the cumulative effect of suppressed evidence, a state court does not unreasonably apply Kyles simply because it stresses the strength of the remaining case so long as it ultimately assesses whether there is a “reasonable probability” of a different result. Given Richter’s “fairminded jurist” deference, the Maryland appellate court’s conclusion that the withheld impeachment would not have undermined confidence in the verdict falls within the range of reasonable applications of Brady/Kyles, and the federal court’s reweighing resembles the kind of substitution AEDPA forbids.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under AEDPA, federal habeas relief is available when a state court decision involves an “unreasonable application” of clearly established Supreme Court law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Williams v. Taylor. Kyles v. Whitley clearly establishes that Brady materiality is a cumulative, whole-case inquiry and “is not a sufficiency of evidence test,” requiring courts to assess whether the suppressed evidence, considered collectively with the trial record, undermines confidence in the verdict. By treating materiality as satisfied so long as “substantial” remaining evidence supported conviction—rather than adding the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence to the defense case and subtracting its force from the prosecution’s—the Maryland appellate court unreasonably applied Kyles’ governing framework, notwithstanding AEDPA deference under Harrington v. Richter.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: AEDPA permits relief only if the state court’s decision involved an unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law, 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), but Brady materiality as articulated in Kyles requires a holistic assessment of the suppressed evidence’s cumulative effect on the entire case and expressly “is not a sufficiency of evidence test.” Here, the Maryland appellate court’s analysis—cataloguing the remaining evidence “connecting” Martin to the crime and concluding it was still “strong,” while not grappling with how the suppressed report would have reshaped the prosecution’s theory, aided alternative defense theories, or affected key instructional inferences—tracks the Kyles dissent’s rejected approach rather than Kyles’s controlling rule. Strickler does not authorize substituting a “still enough evidence” rationale for the Kyles cumulative-in-context inquiry, and under Williams v. Taylor and Harrington v. Richter, that methodological departure can be an unreasonable application when it fails to apply the governing materiality framework. Because the state court effectively treated materiality like a sufficiency-of-the-evidence inquiry, its application of clearly established Brady precedent was unreasonable under § 2254(d)(1).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: AEDPA permits relief only if the state court’s decision was contrary to, or involved an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Williams v. Taylor. Clearly established Brady materiality—especially as articulated in Kyles v. Whitley—requires a cumulative, whole-case inquiry into whether the suppressed evidence creates a “reasonable probability” of a different result, not a sufficiency-of-the-evidence determination that other evidence could still support the verdict. If the Maryland appellate court effectively treated materiality as satisfied whenever “substantial” remaining evidence supported conviction, it unreasonably applied Kyles’ governing rule notwithstanding any correct verbal recitation of the standard, see Rompilla v. Beard, and AEDPA deference does not extend to substituting a sufficiency test for the required cumulative materiality analysis.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under AEDPA, federal habeas relief is available only if the state court’s adjudication was an “unreasonable application” of clearly established Supreme Court law, not merely incorrect. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Harrington v. Richter; Lockyer v. Andrade. Although Kyles v. Whitley requires Brady materiality to be assessed cumulatively and not as a pure sufficiency-of-the-evidence inquiry, the state appellate court articulated the correct “undermine confidence in the verdict” standard and its bottom-line conclusion can be reasonable given the remaining evidence, which is enough to preclude relief so long as fairminded jurists could agree. Richter and Williams v. Taylor caution that AEDPA deference applies to the result and does not permit federal courts to reweigh evidence and demand a more “nuanced” written analysis when the state court’s decision is within the bounds of reasonableness.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), federal habeas relief is barred unless the state court’s decision is contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law. Kyles v. Whitley clearly establishes that Brady materiality is a cumulative, whole-case inquiry and “is not a sufficiency of evidence test,” requiring assessment of the suppressed evidence’s combined effect on the verdict rather than whether the remaining evidence could still support guilt. If the Maryland appellate court effectively treated materiality as “other evidence was enough,” without integrating the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory proof into the total evidentiary picture as Kyles and Strickler v. Greene require, that is a methodological misapplication of the governing rule—not merely a reasonable disagreement about weight—satisfying AEDPA’s ‘unreasonable application’ standard as articulated in Williams v. Taylor and Harrington v. Richter. Given the clearly established anti-sufficiency principle in Kyles, fairminded jurists would not endorse a materiality analysis that functionally collapses into sufficiency review.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under AEDPA, federal habeas relief is warranted when a state court unreasonably applies clearly established Supreme Court law, 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), not merely when it reaches a debatable result. Clearly established Brady materiality doctrine requires assessing the suppressed evidence cumulatively and in light of the whole record, and it is legal error to treat materiality as a sufficiency-of-the-evidence inquiry that asks only whether the remaining evidence could still support the verdict. Kyles v. Whitley makes this rule “clear” and rejects the very mode of analysis that inventories inculpatory evidence while failing to add the suppressed evidence to the defense case and subtract its impeachment force from the prosecution’s case; Strickler v. Greene does not authorize a “remaining evidence was enough” shortcut where impeachment of a key witness could reshape the prosecution’s theory and the jury’s deliberations. Given that misapplication of Kyles’ holistic framework, the Maryland appellate court’s approach falls outside the range of fairminded adjudication contemplated by Harrington v. Richter and Williams v. Taylor, so Respondent is entitled to relief.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, under AEDPA, the Maryland appellate court unreasonably applied clearly established Supreme Court Brady materiality law by treating materiality like a sufficiency-of-the-evidence inquiry instead of evaluating the cumulative effect of suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence on the trial as a whole.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d) (AEDPA deference standard) as applied to the Due Process Brady doctrine (U.S. Const. amend. XIV) requiring disclosure of material exculpatory/impeachment evidence.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (state officials) argue that federal habeas relief is barred by AEDPA because the state court articulated the correct Brady/Kyles standard and reasonably found the suppressed evidence not material in light of the remaining trial evidence; they rely in part on Strickler to contend that even with additional impeachment the verdict would stand, and maintain that the Fourth Circuit (or lower federal court) improperly second-guessed the state court’s materiality determination rather than asking whether it was beyond the bounds of fairminded disagreement.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Martin) argues that although the Maryland appellate court recited Kyles, it unreasonably applied it by effectively asking whether the remaining evidence was sufficient to convict—an approach Kyles labels legal error—and by failing to perform the required holistic, cumulative assessment that adds the suppressed evidence to the defense side and subtracts the force of the State’s case after impeachment; respondent also argues Strickler is distinguishable because in Strickler the remaining evidence was largely unaffected and the impeached witness was not central in the same way, whereas here impeachment of a key prosecution witness (Carter) would have substantially weakened the State’s proof and its theory as presented to the jury.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan press the hardest point: under Kyles and Williams, a state court cannot avoid Brady’s cumulative materiality inquiry by effectively doing a “remaining evidence” sufficiency analysis while reciting the right words. But Richter and Lockyer instruct that § 2254(d)(1) asks whether the state court’s bottom-line no-materiality determination is beyond fairminded disagreement, and discussion of the strength of other evidence can still be part of Strickler’s confidence-in-the-verdict assessment rather than an impermissible sufficiency test. Even if Maryland’s explanation was methodologically imperfect, I do not see clearly established law requiring federal habeas relief whenever a state opinion sounds in “remaining evidence” terms, so long as a fairminded jurist could still conclude the suppressed material was largely cumulative impeachment and did not undermine confidence. On minimalist, institution-preserving grounds, I would reverse the grant of habeas without deciding the Brady question de novo.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan press the best opposing point: Kyles requires a cumulative materiality assessment and Williams teaches that lip service to the right words cannot mask application of the wrong test. But Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s Richter/Andrade response is decisive under the text of § 2254(d)(1): we ask whether the state court’s no-“reasonable probability” result is beyond fairminded disagreement, not whether its opinion reads like an ideal Kyles analysis. Kyles does not clearly establish that a state court’s discussion of the strength of the remaining record—when tied to confidence-in-the-verdict language—necessarily collapses into an impermissible sufficiency test, and Strickler confirms that additional impeachment often will not undermine confidence in a verdict. On this record, at minimum, a fairminded jurist could conclude the suppressed material was not outcome-altering, so AEDPA forecloses habeas relief even if Maryland’s reasoning was imperfect.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan offer the strongest opposing point: under Kyles and Williams, a court cannot recite “reasonable probability” yet operationally apply a sufficiency-style “remaining evidence is substantial” test, and that methodological substitution can be an unreasonable application. But Richter and Lockyer, as the Chief Justice stresses, make the AEDPA question about whether the state court’s no-materiality result is beyond fairminded disagreement, and Kyles does not clearly establish that any consideration of the strength of the remaining record—alongside the confidence-in-the-verdict formulation—amounts to a forbidden sufficiency test. Strickler reinforces that additional impeachment (even if helpful) can be immaterial where it is cumulative or does not meaningfully alter the verdict calculus, and a fairminded jurist could view the suppressed material that way here. Treating Maryland’s imperfect articulation as per se unreasonableness would, in practical consequence, convert § 2254(d)(1) into error-correction and undermine finality in criminal judgments beyond what Congress authorized.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s strongest point—echoed by Justices Alito and Kavanaugh—is that Richter/Andrade require deference to the state court’s bottom-line result even if its reasoning is inartful, so long as any fairminded jurist could agree. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan stress, Kyles clearly establishes that Brady materiality is not a sufficiency-style “the remaining evidence is strong” inquiry; when a court operationally treats materiality as near-synonymous with residual sufficiency, Williams teaches that reciting the right words does not cure the use of the wrong test. Strickler does not change that analysis here because it addresses genuinely marginal, cumulative impeachment, whereas this suppression alters the credibility architecture the jury used to assess the State’s narrative, demanding the holistic recalibration Kyles requires. Under my pragmatic, fairness-focused approach, permitting a sufficiency proxy to pass as “reasonable” would hollow out Brady in precisely the credibility-driven cases where wrongful convictions most threaten the vulnerable.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s Richter/Andrade point seriously: § 2254(d)(1) asks whether a fairminded jurist could sustain the no-materiality result, not whether the state court wrote a model opinion. But Williams v. Taylor matters here in the way Justice Barrett emphasizes—reciting Brady/Kyles language does not insulate a decision that functionally uses a different test—and Maryland’s analysis reads like a catalog of “remaining evidence” rather than the Kyles-required cumulative recalibration with the suppressed evidence added to the mix. Justice Alito is right that considering the overall strength of the record can be part of materiality, yet Kyles clearly distinguishes that holistic confidence-in-the-verdict inquiry from a sufficiency proxy; if the court never meaningfully integrates how the suppression reconfigures witness credibility and the State’s narrative architecture, deference does not extend to that methodological misapplication. Strickler (invoked by Roberts and Thomas) confirms incremental impeachment can be immaterial, but it does not authorize skipping Kyles’s whole-case assessment when the withheld material plausibly changes the credibility calculus that drives the verdict.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s Richter/Andrade point is the hardest for my position: § 2254(d)(1) asks whether a fairminded jurist could reach the same result, not whether the state court wrote a model opinion. But as Justice Barrett stresses, Kyles clearly establishes that Brady materiality is not a sufficiency-of-the-remaining-evidence inquiry; if the Maryland court functionally treated “the rest of the case is strong” as dispositive without the required cumulative, whole-record recalibration, Williams v. Taylor allows us to deem that an unreasonable application even if the right words were recited. Justice Alito’s concern about turning AEDPA into error correction is real, yet this is not mere inartful reasoning—on this record the state court’s method appears to operationalize the wrong test in a way that can alter the materiality conclusion. Strickler, invoked by the Chief and Justice Thomas, doesn’t change that because it addresses genuinely marginal impeachment; here the withheld evidence seems to strike at the credibility architecture and thus the confidence-in-the-verdict judgment Kyles demands.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s best point is that Maryland’s discussion sounds like the sufficiency-style shortcut Kyles rejects, and Williams confirms that reciting the right words does not immunize an operationally wrong test. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that Richter/Andrade focus our § 2254(d)(1) inquiry on whether any fairminded jurist could agree with the state court’s bottom-line “no reasonable probability” conclusion, not whether the opinion modeled Kyles’s preferred analytic form. Even if Maryland imperfectly framed its reasoning by emphasizing “remaining evidence,” Kyles and Strickler still permit looking to the whole record to decide whether confidence is undermined, and I cannot say—on this record—that the no-materiality result crosses Richter’s “beyond fairminded disagreement” line. Institutionally, treating methodological slippage alone as unreasonableness risks converting AEDPA into de novo Brady error-correction, which Richter cautions against.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Richter/Andrade point is the hardest: AEDPA asks whether any fairminded jurist could agree with the state court’s bottom-line no-materiality result, and it does not authorize us to grade the opinion’s craftsmanship. But Williams v. Taylor makes clear that parroting the right Brady/Kyles formulation does not insulate a decision that functionally applies a different test, and Kyles clearly rejects treating materiality as a catalog of “remaining evidence” rather than a cumulative, whole-case recalibration with the suppressed evidence added. Here, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, Maryland’s reasoning reads less like a confidence-in-the-verdict judgment and more like a sufficiency proxy that never integrates the suppressed report’s exculpatory/impeachment force into the overall narrative—an error of method Kyles forbids, not mere inartful phrasing. Strickler’s discussion of incremental impeachment may support a no-materiality outcome in some records, but it cannot supply a reasonable basis where the state court fails to conduct the Kyles-required cumulative assessment of how credibility architecture shifts.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s Richter/Andrade point seriously: AEDPA asks whether a fairminded jurist could agree with the result, not whether the state court wrote a model opinion. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan stress, Kyles clearly establishes that materiality is a cumulative, whole-case recalibration—not a “remaining evidence is strong” proxy—and Williams v. Taylor recognizes that parroting the correct standard does not insulate a decision that functionally applies the wrong test. Here, the state court’s analysis appears to do precisely what Kyles forbids by treating the inquiry as whether the residual case could still support conviction rather than integrating how the suppressed material would alter the credibility architecture of the prosecution’s narrative. Under my procedural-fairness, consequence-attentive approach, allowing that methodological failure to pass as mere inartful reasoning would systematically dilute Brady in cases where credibility is decisive, and that is beyond fairminded disagreement on this record.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), federal habeas relief is unavailable unless the state court’s Brady ruling was an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established law, not merely incorrect. Kyles v. Whitley makes clear that Brady materiality “is not a sufficiency of evidence test” and requires a cumulative, whole-case assessment, but AEDPA (Harrington v. Richter; Lockyer v. Andrade; Woods v. Donald) demands deference where the state court recited the correct standard and its analysis—however inartful—can be understood as concluding there was no “reasonable probability” of a different result. Given that Strickler v. Greene recognizes that additional impeachment often does not suffice where the remaining evidence supports the verdict, I cannot say the Maryland court’s materiality determination was beyond fairminded disagreement. The narrow, institutionally modest course is therefore to reverse federal habeas relief rather than expand error-correction under AEDPA.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), federal habeas relief is barred unless the state court’s decision was not merely wrong, but an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established Supreme Court law, and fairminded jurists must be unable to disagree. Although Kyles v. Whitley makes clear that Brady materiality is assessed cumulatively and “is not a sufficiency of evidence test,” the relevant question under Harrington v. Richter and Lockyer v. Andrade is whether the Maryland appellate court’s application of the reasonable-probability standard was beyond the bounds of fairminded disagreement, not whether a federal court would weigh the record differently. Given that the state court articulated the correct Brady framework and concluded the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory material would not undermine confidence in the verdict in light of the remaining evidence, AEDPA requires deference even if its reasoning could be phrased differently. On that constrained standard, Respondent has not shown the kind of extreme malfunction in the state criminal process that § 2254(d) permits federal courts to remedy.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), federal habeas relief is barred unless the Maryland court’s Brady materiality ruling was not merely wrong but an unreasonable application of clearly established law. Even if the state court’s discussion resembled a sufficiency analysis in places, AEDPA directs review of the decision’s reasonableness, not the precision of its reasoning, and relief is unavailable so long as there is a reasonable basis to conclude the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence did not create a reasonable probability of a different result. Harrington v. Richter requires denying relief where “fairminded jurists could disagree,” and given the remaining inculpatory evidence and Strickler’s recognition that additional impeachment often will not be material, the state court’s no-materiality determination falls within the bounds of reasonable adjudication. Kyles v. Whitley’s cumulative-assessment instruction is clearly established, but it does not authorize federal courts to redo the state court’s weighing de novo when the state court could reasonably conclude the verdict would stand.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under AEDPA, § 2254(d)(1) still requires that the state court’s application of clearly established Brady law be reasonable, not merely that it recite the right words. Kyles v. Whitley makes clear that materiality is not a sufficiency-of-the-evidence test and instead demands a cumulative, holistic assessment of how suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence would affect the jury’s view of the case and confidence in the verdict. If the Maryland appellate court effectively upheld the conviction by cataloging remaining inculpatory proof while failing to add the suppressed evidence to the defense case and account for its impeaching force against a key witness, that is the kind of misapplication Kyles condemns and can be “unreasonable” even under Harrington v. Richter’s fairminded-disagreement standard. Strickler does not insulate the decision where the suppressed material would meaningfully undercut the State’s narrative and the credibility of central testimony, particularly in a case hinging on witness reliability and contested inferences.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: AEDPA permits relief only if the state court’s decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1). Under Kyles v. Whitley, Brady materiality “is not a sufficiency of evidence test” and instead requires a cumulative, whole-case assessment of whether the suppressed evidence undermines confidence in the verdict. If the Maryland appellate court effectively asked only whether the remaining evidence was still “substantial” or sufficient to convict—without integrating the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory material into the overall evidentiary picture—that is the kind of misapplication Kyles forbids and can be unreasonable under Williams v. Taylor even given Richter’s fairminded-disagreement deference.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: AEDPA permits relief only if the state court’s decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Williams v. Taylor; Harrington v. Richter. Kyles makes clear that Brady materiality “is not a sufficiency of evidence test” and requires assessing the cumulative effect of all suppressed exculpatory and impeachment evidence on the verdict, not merely listing remaining inculpatory proof. If the Maryland appellate court effectively treated materiality as a sufficiency inquiry and failed to conduct the holistic Kyles cumulative assessment, that constitutes an unreasonable application of clearly established Brady/Kyles law notwithstanding its recitation of the correct standard.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), federal habeas relief is unavailable unless the state court’s Brady materiality determination was not just wrong but “beyond any possibility for fairminded disagreement.” Harrington v. Richter; Lockyer v. Andrade. Even accepting Kyles’s instruction that materiality is “not a sufficiency of evidence test” and requires a cumulative, whole-trial assessment, Kyles v. Whitley, a state court does not unreasonably apply clearly established law merely because it discusses the strength of the remaining evidence while concluding there is no “reasonable probability” of a different result. Given AEDPA’s deference and this Court’s caution against treating habeas as error-correction (Woods v. Donald; Bell v. Cone), I would not hold that the Maryland appellate court’s application of Brady/Kyles crossed the Richter threshold here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), the question is whether the state court’s Brady decision was an unreasonable application of clearly established law, not whether the federal court would reach a different result. Kyles v. Whitley clearly establishes that Brady materiality “is not a sufficiency of evidence test” and requires assessing the cumulative effect of suppressed evidence on the verdict, considering how it would alter the overall evidentiary picture. If, as the record indicates, the Maryland appellate court effectively asked only whether the remaining evidence was still “substantial” or sufficient to convict, it misapplied Kyles’ holistic reasonable-probability framework in a way that can be unreasonable under Williams v. Taylor and Harrington v. Richter. Given that the suppressed forensic report bore directly on impeaching a key prosecution witness and strengthening the defense narrative, the failure to conduct a cumulative, trial-wide assessment falls beyond fairminded disagreement under AEDPA.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a state court can recite the correct rule yet still "unreasonably apply" it, 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Williams v. Taylor and Rompilla v. Beard make that clear. Kyles v. Whitley holds that Brady materiality is a holistic, cumulative inquiry into whether there is a reasonable probability of a different result and "is not a sufficiency of evidence test," so a state court that effectively asks whether the remaining evidence could still support conviction misapplies clearly established law. If Maryland’s appellate reasoning treated the suppressed impeachment/exculpatory evidence as immaterial because other evidence "connected" the defendant to the crime—without subtracting the force of the State’s case after impeachment and adding the defense value cumulatively—then, as in Kyles (and unlike Strickler’s largely unaffected remaining proof), that approach falls beyond fairminded disagreement and warrants habeas relief. Procedural fairness in criminal trials requires enforcing Brady’s disclosure duty where suppression undermines confidence in the verdict.
